title: A Survey on Swarming With Micro Air Vehicles: Fundamental Challenges and Constraints

subsections.content:
Micro air vehicles (MAVs) occupy a distinctive regime in aerial robotics: they operate under severe size, weight, and power constraints, yet offer access to cluttered three-dimensional workspaces that are difficult for both ground robots and larger UAVs. Early quadrotor surveys established the platform’s appeal through mechanical simplicity, hover capability, and compatibility with lightweight sensing and feedback control, while also highlighting persistent limits in endurance, payload, and onboard computation ref [1], ref [2]. These constraints largely explain why multirotors—especially quadrotors and small hexarotors—became the dominant research substrate for aerial swarms rather than fixed-wing or more bioinspired morphologies ref [1], ref [2], ref [6].

Within this landscape, swarm robotics extends the single-MAV autonomy problem toward collective behaviors such as formation flight, cooperative exploration, distributed sensing, and task allocation. Foundational demonstrations such as SFly emphasized onboard vision, SLAM-enabled navigation, cooperative mapping, and optimized surveillance positioning for teams of MAVs ref [7]. Subsequent experimental platforms pushed scale and agility: agile micro-quadrotor teams showed dense indoor formation flight with external localization and coordinated trajectory generation for up to 20 vehicles ref [4], while Crazyswarm demonstrated that nano-quadcopter swarms could scale to dozens of vehicles by moving estimation, control, and portions of planning onboard and by carefully engineering communication and tracking pipelines ref [5].

Recent aerial swarm surveys make clear that the field now spans a broad spectrum, from tightly coordinated laboratory collectives to outdoor, partially decentralized systems, but the central tension remains unchanged: swarm-level capability emerges only when platform design, perception, communication, and control are co-optimized under MAV-scale constraints ref [6], ref [2]. Accordingly, the MAV and swarm robotics landscape is best viewed not as a simple progression in team size, but as a convergence of hardware miniaturization, autonomy stacks, and collective coordination methods that jointly determine what real-world swarming is feasible ref [2], ref [4], ref [5], ref [6].

subsections.subsection_title: Robustness, Safety, and Embodied Resilience in Real-World Operation
subsections.content:
Robust real-world MAV swarms must tolerate not only algorithmic uncertainty, but also perception dropouts, collisions, and partial vehicle damage. At the single-robot level, resilience has been demonstrated through autonomous re-initialization and failure recovery after visual-estimation loss, enabling continued flight rather than immediate landing or human takeover ref [7]. More generally, learned reactive navigation in cluttered environments and large-scale self-supervised crash data showed that useful avoidance behavior can emerge from failure-rich experience, albeit with clear dependence on sensing quality and scene structure ref [12], ref [14]. These works emphasize that robustness is not merely a controller property; it is an operational capability to degrade gracefully and recover autonomy after estimation or policy breakdown.

A complementary line of work treats collision as a design condition rather than an exceptional event. Collision-tolerant MAVs such as AirBurr explicitly exploit contacts and self-righting to resume operation after impacts ref [9], while insect-inspired multicopters use dual-stiffness structures and energy-absorbing materials to survive high-speed collisions with limited permanent damage ref [8]. Similar ideas extend to lighter-than-air platforms, where compliant micro-airships can sustain repeated inter-vehicle and wall contacts while still reaching waypoints, suggesting an alternative safety regime based on low kinetic energy and benign impact dynamics ref [10]. For swarm systems, such embodied resilience can reduce the need for perfect separation and can localize failures instead of cascading them across the team.

Safety margins are nevertheless bounded by sensing and actuation latency. Formal analysis of high-speed sense-and-avoid shows that admissible flight speed depends jointly on perception delay, sensing range, and available lateral acceleration, making low-latency sensing central to safe operation in dense environments ref [11]. This has direct swarm implications: as platform count grows, uncertainty in relative state, collision risk, and recovery interactions all increase, so robustness must be co-designed across mechanics, estimation, and operating envelope. In practice, resilient swarms will likely combine conservative speed selection, recoverable estimation pipelines, and mechanically forgiving airframes rather than rely on obstacle avoidance alone ref [7], ref [8], ref [9], ref [11].

subsections.subsection_title: System-Level Co-Design of Airframes, Platforms, and Modularity
subsections.content:
System-level co-design in MAV swarms is fundamentally a problem of matching morphology, actuation, sensing, and computation to collective operating modes rather than optimizing each subsystem in isolation. Open, lightweight research platforms such as Crazyflie 2.0 have been especially influential because they expose this coupling between payload, endurance, onboard compute, and swarm reproducibility, while also enabling rapid hardware and firmware iteration at scale ref [16]. At the other extreme, designs explicitly optimized for small size, human safety, and collision tolerance show that airframe geometry, protective structures, and control authority must be co-designed if dense multi-robot operation is to remain practical outside ideal laboratory conditions ref [9].

A second line of work treats morphology itself as a controllable resource. Foldable and transformable quadrotors demonstrate that negotiating clutter, inspection stand-off, and manipulation opportunities can be improved by changing shape in flight, but only when controller adaptation and control allocation are redesigned around morphology-dependent inertia and thrust mapping ref [14]. This observation generalizes to swarm systems: platform versatility is not merely a mechanical attribute, but an architectural property emerging from joint design of frame kinematics, actuation limits, estimation assumptions, and mission envelope.

Modularity further extends co-design from the vehicle to the aggregate. The Distributed Flight Array showed early that individually simple modules can gain aerial functionality through physical interconnection, provided docking, distributed communication, and cooperative control are designed together ref [18]. More recent systems such as ModQuad and aerial modules for inflight self-disassembly push this logic toward self-assembling and reconfigurable flying structures, where attachment mechanisms, module geometry, force distribution, and disassembly maneuvers are inseparable from stability and scalability considerations ref [19], ref [7]. Across these examples, the central lesson is that swarm-capable MAV platforms benefit from modular interfaces and morphology-aware control only when the entire stack—airframe, electronics, software, and reconfiguration mechanism—is co-optimized from the outset.

subsections.subsection_title: Interdependence of Flight Dynamics, Estimation, and Navigation
subsections.content:
For MAVs, flight dynamics, state estimation, and navigation cannot be designed as separable layers: aerodynamic coupling, vibration, and aggressive attitude changes directly shape estimator observability and, in turn, the feasible navigation envelope. Early MEMS-based navigation systems already exposed this coupling, showing that small-airframe operation requires estimator architectures that remain functional under vibration, magnetic disturbance, GPS shadowing, and hover-specific dynamics rather than assuming benign aircraft conditions ref [21]. Complementary-filter formulations made this dependence explicit by treating navigation as bandwidth matching across heterogeneous sensors, with vehicle kinematics entering the filter structure itself ref [25].

This interdependence is strongest in GPS-denied flight, where control authority depends on timely, drift-bounded onboard state feedback. Vision-based MAV systems demonstrated that autonomous stabilization and waypoint flight emerge only when visual odometry or SLAM, inertial sensing, and platform timing are co-designed, including scale observability, latency, and sensor-to-body calibration ref [22]. Visual-inertial fusion frameworks further showed that self-calibration, excitation conditions, and distributed computation between flight-control and onboard processors are not implementation details but determinants of navigational robustness ref [22]. Multi-sensor fusion across indoor and outdoor transitions extends this logic: relative and absolute measurements from cameras, lasers, IMUs, altimeters, magnetometers, and GPS must be fused while preserving consistency under delayed and out-of-order updates ref [17].

At the micro scale, estimator design is also constrained by sensing modality and airframe-specific aerodynamics. Quadrotor-aware drift-free velocity estimation exploits rotor-induced dynamics and accelerometer behavior unavailable to generic inertial filters, improving attitude and horizontal-velocity estimates for closed-loop flight ref [13]. Likewise, lightweight optical-flow and stereo pipelines illustrate that navigation performance depends on matching perception algorithms to onboard compute, field of view, and obstacle-avoidance needs, not merely on algorithmic accuracy in isolation ref [15]. Overall, reliable MAV navigation is a system property: airframe dynamics determine what can be estimated, estimator quality bounds navigational aggressiveness, and navigation objectives feed back into sensing and control architecture choices ref [21], ref [22], ref [17].

subsections.subsection_title: Swarm Coordination, Communication, and Collective Reliability
subsections.content:
Swarm coordination in MAV systems is inseparable from the communication and estimation substrates that sustain local interaction. In GPS-denied settings, cooperative relative localization based on ultra-wideband ranging and exchanged self-motion estimates has enabled distributed inter-robot state inference, reducing dependence on external infrastructure while preserving the locality needed for scalable coordination ref [28]. This complements vision-based onboard state estimation in swarms of quadrotors, where fully onboard visual-inertial odometry has supported coordinated formation flight without motion capture or GPS, but also exposes how estimation drift, bandwidth limits, and asynchronous updates become collective—not merely individual—failure modes ref [32].

At the coordination layer, real-world flocking studies show that collective behavior is strongly constrained by vehicle dynamics and communication range. For fixed-wing platforms, coherent Reynolds-style flocking emerges only when turn-rate limits and link range are jointly sufficient to maintain interaction neighborhoods over time ref [29]. In confined spaces, more realistic flocking models must additionally account for delays, obstacle interactions, stochastic communication dropouts, and acceleration limits; evolutionary tuning has proven effective for identifying parameter regimes that remain stable for larger groups and higher speeds, including outdoor demonstrations with dozens of drones ref [31]. Large-scale field trials with 50 fixed-wing UAVs further underline that launch, ingress/egress procedures, ad hoc networking, and operator workload are system-level determinants of swarm reliability, not peripheral implementation details ref [9].

Collective reliability is therefore best understood probabilistically and across multiple layers. Team-level mission success can improve with redundancy even when individual robots are less reliable, but only if communication, timing, and task coupling do not introduce common-mode failures ref [26]. At the opposite end of the design spectrum, collision-tolerant pico-quadrotor swarms suggest that embodied resilience can partially substitute for precise avoidance and heavy coordination, enabling useful collective behavior despite impacts, sparse sensing, and limited planning ref [10]. For MAV swarms, the central design tension is thus not simply centralized versus distributed control, but how much collective performance can be preserved under degraded links, imperfect relative state, and inevitable individual failures.

subsections.section_title: Relative Perception, Communication, and Safety in Multi-MAV Interaction
subsections.subsection_title: Vision-Based Detection, Tracking, and Collaborative State Estimation
subsections.content:
Vision-based multi-MAV interaction has progressed from marker-aided swarm demonstrations to fully onboard relative pose estimation and collaborative mapping. Early systems for indoor competitions showed that lightweight monocular pipelines could support decentralized mission execution when coupled with marker-based localization, EKF fusion, and obstacle mapping, although with strong environmental assumptions ref [35]. Beyond such structured settings, vision-only distributed formation control has been demonstrated without external positioning by combining onboard cameras and IMU measurements to recover relative pose from shared scene observations, including homography-based rectification and consensus over scale, thereby linking perception directly to closed-loop coordination ref [33]. Recent cooperative target-detection work further broadened the design space by using deep networks for airborne UAV detection and tracking, where visual processing is aided by exchanged navigation hints to improve robustness against clutter, illumination changes, and range variation ref [34].

A central challenge is turning pairwise observations into swarm-level state estimates. Collaborative visual SLAM systems address this by sharing keyframes, descriptors, landmarks, or summarized map information across agents to improve robustness and consistency ref [37]. Early centralized monocular approaches for multiple MAVs streamed selected keyframes and relative pose estimates to a ground station, where separate maps were built and merged upon overlap detection, enabling a common global frame while preserving lightweight onboard odometry ref [8]. More recent systems push this collaboration toward greater communication efficiency: decentralized visual SLAM uses compact image descriptors and selective geometric verification to reduce place-recognition traffic, while distributed smoothing and mapping methods preserve consistency when information is shared across robots ref [38], ref [39].

Overall, the literature reveals a trade-off between estimation quality, onboard autonomy, and communication burden. Centralized collaborative SLAM remains attractive for micro-air-vehicle teams because it simplifies map fusion and loop closure ref [8], whereas decentralized formulations better match scalable swarms but must carefully control data association, synchronization, and information double counting ref [37], ref [38], ref [39]. Thus, vision-based detection and tracking in multi-MAV systems should be viewed not as isolated perception modules, but as tightly coupled components of collaborative state estimation architectures that determine whether relative sensing can scale from pairwise interaction to persistent swarm operation ref [33], ref [34], ref [37].

subsections.section_title: Relative Perception, Communication, and Safety in Multi-MAV Interaction
subsections.subsection_title: Communication Frameworks and Networking for Swarm Coordination
subsections.content:
Communication is a primary systems bottleneck for MAV swarms because strict size-weight-power budgets, intermittent line-of-sight, and highly dynamic network topology jointly constrain both control-loop closure and shared situational awareness. Existing surveys broadly distinguish centralized infrastructure-based architectures, fully ad hoc flying networks, and hybrid schemes, each implying different tradeoffs in latency, robustness, and autonomy ref [7]. Early airborne sensor-network demonstrations such as SensorFlock already highlighted that link quality in MAV teams is strongly state dependent, with air-to-air propagation differing substantially from ground links and multi-hop performance being sensitive to relaying and packet loss ref [10].

At the physical and MAC layers, protocol choice remains application-specific. Comparative studies of Bluetooth, UWB, ZigBee, and Wi-Fi emphasize the familiar tradeoff between throughput, range, protocol complexity, and power, with ZigBee/Bluetooth favoring low-rate low-power exchange and Wi-Fi/UWB supporting heavier telemetry or payload streams ref [43]. Bluetooth 5 improves range, broadcast capacity, and IoT-oriented features, making it attractive for lightweight inter-robot messaging, although contention and topology management still limit dense fast-moving swarms ref [9]. In practice, swarm-enabling platforms often adopt low-cost mesh radios and modular onboard computing to support decentralized state exchange and behavior execution without external infrastructure ref [8].

Above the link layer, swarm coordination depends not only on connectivity but also on how information is structured and when it is disseminated. Information-exchange design patterns such as broadcaster, local exchange, storage, and exchange-center mechanisms provide a useful abstraction for matching communication policies to task density, spatial dispersion, and robustness requirements ref [44]. For larger-area operations, cellular and emerging 5G machine-to-machine backbones have been proposed as hybrid infrastructures that extend range and offload networking complexity while retaining distributed decision making onboard the vehicles ref [7]. Overall, effective communication frameworks for multi-MAV swarms must co-design protocol, topology control, and information-sharing policy with mission timescales rather than treating networking as a transparent substrate ref [7], ref [8], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Relative Perception, Communication, and Safety in Multi-MAV Interaction
subsections.subsection_title: Collective Motion and Flocking Under Relative Sensing
subsections.content:
Collective motion under relative sensing is rooted in distributed flocking laws that replace global trajectory assignment with local interaction rules. The canonical formulation is Reynolds’ alignment–cohesion–separation model, which remains the conceptual basis for many MAV swarm controllers despite its original animation focus ref [28]. Control-theoretic work subsequently formalized related behaviors for stable aggregation through attraction/repulsion interaction laws, showing how odd pairwise forces can guarantee bounded cohesive motion without prescribing a rigid formation ref [46]. For MAV swarms, this distinction is important: under limited relative sensing, maintaining group coherence and heading consensus is often more realistic than exact geometry control.

In aerial robotics, the main challenge is that flocking rules must be embedded in strongly constrained vehicle dynamics and sparse local measurements. Fixed-wing experiments demonstrated that Reynolds-style flocking can be realized outdoors, but only when communication range is commensurate with turning authority; otherwise the swarm fragments or fails to align ref [49]. Stochastic optimal-control formulations for fixed-wing UAVs extend this idea by explicitly accounting for actuation uncertainty and relative leader–follower state, enabling flocking that serves a sensing objective rather than motion alone ref [7]. More broadly, self-propelled-particle and consensus-based flocking analyses clarify how connectivity, neighborhood topology, and nonholonomic constraints shape convergence and coherence under local interactions ref [6], ref [8], ref [9].

An important direction for micro-scale platforms is flocking without absolute positioning. Evolutionary and behavior-based approaches show that useful swarming can emerge from onboard relative cues alone, including communication-relay behaviors and collective motion without explicit localization ref [10], ref [48]. This is especially relevant for GPS-denied or low-payload MAVs, where relative bearing, proximity, or encounter-based signals may be the only scalable sensing modality. Overall, flocking under relative sensing offers a lightweight route to coordinated coverage and mobility, but its robustness depends critically on the coupling between sensing range, update rate, communication intermittency, and vehicle agility ref [46], ref [49], ref [7].

subsections.section_title: Relative Perception, Communication, and Safety in Multi-MAV Interaction
subsections.subsection_title: Collision Avoidance and Safe Multi-MAV Navigation
subsections.content:
Collision avoidance in multi-MAV systems is shaped by severe sensing, actuation, and computation constraints, which make fully centralized planning difficult and motivate reactive, pairwise-safe schemes. The velocity-obstacle (VO) framework remains a foundational formulation for dynamic environments, representing collision-inducing relative velocities and selecting admissible commands outside these sets ref [10]. Its extension to reciprocal velocity obstacles (RVO) explicitly models the fact that neighboring agents also react, enabling decentralized real-time navigation without explicit negotiation and reducing the oscillations that arise when other MAVs are treated as passive obstacles ref [9].

For aerial swarms, these ideas were further adapted to reciprocal and uncertainty-aware navigation. The hybrid reciprocal velocity obstacle (HRVO) was introduced to suppress reciprocal dances by biasing side selection while retaining the reciprocity assumption, and was validated on physical robots under noisy state estimates and kinematic constraints ref [8]. Such reciprocal methods have directly influenced MAV collision-avoidance designs: ORCA/RVO-style strategies were demonstrated on quadrotors using onboard relative sensing ref [50], while broader quadrotor studies have also shown the need to account for dynamic feasibility, sensing latency, and estimation noise when translating velocity-space commands into safe flight maneuvers ref [50], ref [52].

Beyond vision-only approaches, safe multi-MAV navigation has also been realized with low-cost relative infrastructure and communication-assisted risk reasoning. Commodity quadcopters equipped with ultrasound localization used communicated position/velocity information and dynamically resized risk contours to trigger autonomous intervention only in hazardous situations, highlighting the importance of robustness to localization and communication faults in GNSS-denied operation ref [52]. Overall, the literature indicates a spectrum from purely onboard mutual avoidance to cooperative risk-aware navigation, with the main open challenges being limited field of view, delay-sensitive behavior, conservative safety margins, and scalability under dense encounters ref [50], ref [52], ref [8], ref [9], ref [10].

subsections.section_title: Relative Perception, Communication, and Safety in Multi-MAV Interaction
subsections.content:
Relative localization is a prerequisite for swarm operation in GPS-denied and cluttered environments, yet it is especially difficult on micro air vehicles because payload, computation, and sensing budgets are tightly constrained. The literature therefore spans complementary sensing modalities. Range-based approaches exploit lightweight radios, most prominently UWB, to estimate inter-vehicle distance and fuse it with exchanged motion increments in EKF-like cooperative estimators; this enables decentralized relative positioning over tens of meters, but observability and initialization remain critical, especially when all agents move simultaneously ref [27]. Communication-only solutions push hardware minimalism further by combining RSSI-like ranging with exchanged onboard states, achieving coarse relative localization sufficient for collision avoidance, albeit with lower accuracy and stronger sensitivity to channel disturbances ref [10].

Vision-based mutual perception offers richer geometric constraints. A notable line of work addresses mutual localization from anonymous relative measurements, showing that identifiable tags are not strictly necessary if one exploits multi-view consistency and probabilistic data association; this idea was developed first for anonymous relative measurements in multirobot systems, then for anonymous bearing-only mutual localization in 2-D and 3-D, including UAV experiments ref [14], ref [59], ref [9]. These methods are elegant because they reduce reliance on explicit identity assignment, but they are computationally demanding and remain vulnerable to false positives, missed detections, and symmetry-induced ambiguities. In parallel, practical onboard systems have used passive visual markers for relative localization in GPS-denied MAV groups and formation flight, demonstrating the viability of marker-based mutual perception for compact teams ref [15].

Recent work has increasingly favored active visual beacons that improve robustness outdoors. UVDAR localizes neighboring UAVs using ultraviolet markers, enabling leader-follower control without explicit inter-vehicle communication and maintaining relative position and yaw under varying illumination ref [60]. Its underlying UV-marker framework employs blinking patterns and a 3-D time-position Hough transform to recover both target identity and motion with low computational load, extending operation to challenging indoor/outdoor backgrounds ref [61]. Overall, the trade space is clear: UWB and communication-based methods provide omnidirectional ranging with limited geometric richness ref [27], ref [10], whereas active visual mutual perception offers more informative relative pose estimates but depends on line of sight and marker visibility ref [60], ref [61]. Hybridization across these modalities is therefore a natural direction for robust swarm-scale relative localization.

subsections.section_title: Open Challenges, Operational Deployment, and Outlook
subsections.subsection_title: Persistent Operations: Energy Autonomy, Recharging, and Refueling
subsections.content:
Persistent swarm operation is fundamentally limited by energy logistics: for multirotors, endurance typically remains on the order of minutes, so mission persistence requires either in situ energy harvesting or rapid turnaround on the ground. Solar and fuel-cell concepts show the appeal of moving beyond battery-only architectures, but also expose severe payload, structural, and weather constraints. A fully solar-powered quadcopter has demonstrated controlled out-of-ground-effect flight without onboard storage, albeit only in favorable irradiance and with a fragile, low-margin design ref [62]. Hydrogen fuel-cell VTOL platforms offer much higher specific energy and have been optimized around pressure-tank integration and cruise efficiency, but they introduce safety, redundancy, and hybrid-power-management challenges, especially for VTOL phases ref [8].

For micro air vehicle teams, the near-term deployment path is therefore dominated by automated docking, recharging, and battery replacement infrastructure. Wireless charging reduces mechanical contact requirements and yaw-alignment constraints, and outdoor demonstrations have reported autonomous vision-guided landing with about 75% average wireless power transfer efficiency ref [63]. However, wireless charging remains slower and less power-dense than contact-based approaches, making it better suited to low-power platforms or loosely time-constrained missions ref [63]. Contact-based recharging stations and repeated-sortie autonomy have enabled long-duration operation, including fully autonomous mission cycles with precision landing and recharge over 10 h of operation ref [66].

Battery swapping is often more attractive for swarms because it minimizes downtime and decouples sortie duration from recharge duration. Automated hot-swap systems preserve onboard computation and communication during exchange, with early platforms demonstrating multi-bay charge-and-swap architectures and swap times on the order of 10-30 s in persistent missions ref [65]. Related quadcopter-oriented designs emphasize mechanical simplification, precision landing tolerance, and simultaneous charging of spare packs ref [64]. Yet at swarm scale, open challenges remain in pad scheduling, battery inventory management, health-aware pack assignment, connector wear, localization robustness under wind and dust, and the system-level trade-off between centralized depots and distributed field chargers ref [63], ref [64], ref [65], ref [66].

subsections.section_title: Open Challenges, Operational Deployment, and Outlook
subsections.subsection_title: Fault Detection, Resilience, and System Health in Multi-UAV Teams
subsections.content:
Fault detection in multi-UAV teams remains difficult because faults are expressed through coupled closed-loop interactions rather than isolated component symptoms. Early surveys emphasized that swarm faults span both component faults (e.g., actuators, sensors, controllers) and topology faults (e.g., communication breaks, intrusions), and that scalable diagnosis must therefore be distributed rather than ground-station centric ref [68]. This distinction is especially relevant for MAV swarms, where intermittent links, estimator drift, degraded propulsion, and partial sensing loss can all manifest as collective anomalies rather than immediate crashes.

Recent work has therefore shifted toward decentralized, behavior-based detection schemes that exploit local peer observations. Generic swarm-level methods classify abnormal agents from limited, noisy, and intermittent observations, avoiding dependence on precise plant models or global infrastructure ref [69]. Experimental studies on physical robot swarms further show that behavioral outlier detection can identify multiple sensor and actuator faults online, while remaining tolerant to task changes and reducing false positives through local voting and temporal aggregation ref [70]. Related distributed diagnosis approaches based on observers, residual generation, or cooperative monitoring likewise highlight the value of neighborhood-level redundancy and cross-checking for isolating faulty agents without a single point of failure ref [68], ref [69].

For operational MAV deployments, however, diagnosis must be embedded in a broader resilience and system-health loop. Detection alone is insufficient unless it triggers graceful degradation: controller reconfiguration, task reallocation, exclusion from formation roles, return-to-home, or safe landing. Open problems include distinguishing faults from aggressive maneuvers or environmental disturbances, handling switching topologies and heterogeneous vehicles, detecting latent or intermittent degradation before mission failure, and quantifying team-level health under cascading faults ref [68], ref [69], ref [70]. As swarms scale, health management will likely require hierarchical summaries of local confidence, explicit fault-containment policies, and tight integration with mission planning and assurance frameworks.

subsections.section_title: Open Challenges, Operational Deployment, and Outlook
subsections.content:
Human–swarm interaction remains a central bottleneck for operational deployment because scaling autonomy does not eliminate the need for intent specification, monitoring, and timely intervention. Early work on vision-mediated interaction showed that natural spatial gestures can support selection of individual UAVs and subgroups without reverting to one-to-one teleoperation, thereby shifting the operator toward supervisory rather than direct control ref [71]. More broadly, UAS human–machine interface research has emphasized that small-aircraft control concepts inherited from single-vehicle systems are poorly matched to multi-UAV command, especially when operators must manage sensing, tasking, and safety simultaneously ref [5].

A key open challenge is therefore the design of interfaces that expose swarm-level state and constraints, rather than only raw vehicle telemetry. An ecological approach to supervisory control argues for interfaces that make coverage, energy, mission progress, and failure implications directly perceivable, enabling operators to reason across abstraction levels and improvise during off-nominal events ref [6]. In a four-UAV surveillance study, such ecological displays improved mission-level diagnosis and even supported creative replanning under unexpected battery and wind disturbances, but they also revealed a persistent limitation: control actions still had to be issued largely per vehicle, making interaction labor-intensive as team size grows ref [6].

Looking ahead, effective human–swarm interaction for MAVs will likely require mixed-initiative supervisory control that combines intuitive input modalities, compact mission-centric visualizations, and delegation mechanisms for subgroup formation, replanning, and exception handling ref [71], ref [5], ref [6]. The main unresolved issues are scalability of attention, prevention of automation surprise, and the definition of interface abstractions that remain understandable under communications loss, heterogeneous team behavior, and rapidly changing mission priorities ref [5], ref [6].

subsections.section_title: Open Challenges, Operational Deployment, and Outlook
subsections.subsection_title: Software Stacks, Simulation, and Mission Programming for Deployment
subsections.content:
Operational deployment of MAV swarms remains constrained not only by perception and control, but by the maturity of the surrounding software toolchain. In practice, deployment demands a full stack spanning embedded flight software, middleware, simulation, mission specification, logging, and debugging. Open autopilot frameworks such as PX4 have been influential because they expose modular, node-oriented execution, publish–subscribe communication, and interfaces to ROS/Linux companion computers, thereby supporting both real-time onboard control and higher-level autonomy ref [77]. At the system level, frameworks such as AEROSTACK and ROS-MAGNA move beyond single-vehicle autonomy by organizing mission management, state machines, reusable behaviors, and heterogeneous execution across software-in-the-loop, hardware-in-the-loop, and real vehicles ref [78], ref [80].

Simulation is equally central for deployment readiness, but no single simulator satisfies all swarm requirements. Gazebo established an important open and extensible paradigm for multi-robot simulation and middleware compatibility, yet its original trade-off favored flexibility over very large, visually rich aerial scenes ref [76]. Newer platforms such as AirSim address part of this gap with higher-fidelity rendering, physics, sensor models, and hardware-in-the-loop support for protocols such as MAVLink, which is valuable for perception-driven autonomy and sim-to-real testing ref [8]. Still, the challenge is not just realism, but reproducibility across heterogeneous vehicles, network effects, and mission-scale validation before field use.

Mission programming for swarms also remains an open problem. General robotics middleware offers integration, but swarm deployment benefits from languages and abstractions that directly encode group membership, neighborhood interactions, and decentralized information sharing. Buzz is notable here because it provides explicit constructs for heterogeneous swarm programming while remaining extensible over existing runtimes such as ROS ref [79]. In parallel, protocol-level efforts toward decentralized swarm management over MAVLink highlight the need for standardized commands for grouping, formation control, replacement, and maintenance coordination ref [9]. A key outlook is therefore convergence: linking embedded stacks, simulators, mission managers, and swarm-specific languages into interoperable toolchains that reduce ad hoc engineering and improve certifiable, repeatable deployment ref [77], ref [78], ref [79], ref [80], ref [8], ref [9].

subsections.section_title: Open Challenges, Operational Deployment, and Outlook
subsections.subsection_title: Field Demonstrations, Coordination, and Logistics at Scale
subsections.content:
Field demonstrations remain a crucial filter between laboratory swarming results and deployable multi-MAV systems. Competition-driven and public-field trials have been especially valuable because they expose the coupled difficulties of perception, communication, grasping, and team coordination under setup-time constraints, wind, lighting variation, and partial infrastructure failures. Early vision-based indoor demonstrations already showed that even relatively simple swarms can complete multi-robot missions when coordination is reduced to lightweight state sharing and conservative conflict handling, as in the IMAV 2013 swarm system of ref [83].

More recent outdoor demonstrations, particularly in MBZIRC-style treasure-hunt scenarios, highlight that scaling from a few vehicles to operational teams is less a matter of adding robots than of managing airspace, drop zones, task allocation, and recovery from communication loss. Decentralized search-pick-relocate architectures in ref [82] and collaborative picking-and-delivery systems in ref [35] demonstrate that robust field performance often relies on sectorization of the arena, simple sweep coverage, local visual servoing, and minimal message exchange rather than globally optimal coordination. Likewise, the winning multi-UAV system in ref [5] combined cooperative coverage, explicit waiting and time-window policies around the drop zone, and failure-recovery state machines to keep the team productive despite unreliable Wi-Fi and uneven sensing quality.

These demonstrations collectively suggest that logistics at scale will hinge on support infrastructure as much as on control theory: fast field calibration, repeatable launch/recovery workflows, battery and spares handling, airspace deconfliction, and mission-level replanning when vehicles fail or become unavailable. The literature therefore points toward a pragmatic outlook in which scalable swarm deployment is achieved through layered simplicity—modular autonomy onboard each MAV, constrained interaction protocols, and operational doctrines that degrade gracefully when communication, perception, or individual vehicles underperform [2], ref [35], ref [83], ref [5].
